solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Block off border with sharp spikes

parts.note: to bar off a road is to block it off
a border is a flower bed along the edge of a garden

explanation.surface: Someone fencing off their garden edge with spiky wire.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Border' looks like a fence-line to go with the spikes; here it is the gardener's border, a bed of flowers.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a barb is a sharp backward-pointing spike, so anything fitted with them, like the wire, fits the description.

clue.text: Great leader raised new hatchet to cut tree

indicators.note: the hatchet cuts into the tree, so these letters go inside it

parts.note: the alder is a tree

indicators.note: in a down clue, raising something reads it from bottom to top, so it is turned round

parts.note: an axe is a hatchet

explanation.surface: Someone lifts a brand-new hatchet in order to chop down a tree.
explanation.walkthrough: 'raised' suits a down clue, where a word read upward is reversed; 'Great' is part of the name, not praise.
explanation.definitionFit: Alexander the Great, the Macedonian conqueror, is the leader whose epithet was 'the Great'.

clue.text: In good spirits, you bat second for once after tossing

indicators.note: once the letters have been tossed like a coin they land in a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

indicators.note: second for once means the second letter of the word once

parts.note: its second letter is used

explanation.surface: A cricket captain, having lost the toss, tells a teammate to bat second for a change.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is cricket batting order, but 'second for once' picks a single letter, the second of the word once.
explanation.definitionFit: Buoyant describes someone cheerful and optimistic, whose mood stays up as though floating.

clue.text: Daughters notice chap with an interest in them

definitions.text: chap with an interest in them

parts.note: d is the standard abbreviation for daughter(s), as in family trees
an ad is a notice, an advertisement

explanation.surface: Some girls spotting a man who seems keen on them.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests an admirer; the 'interest' is the fond concern of a father, and 'them' points back to the daughters.
explanation.definitionFit: A cryptic-leaning description: a father naturally cares about his own children, with 'them' pointing back to the daughters in the wordplay.

clue.text: UCAS uncovered shortage, less university space available

indicators.note: with its cover taken off, the word loses its first and last letters

parts.note: the UK university admissions service, used here only for its letters

indicators.note: less means without, so the letter is removed

parts.note: paucity means a shortage

explanation.surface: The admissions service exposes a lack of places now that fewer university spots are open.
explanation.walkthrough: UCAS is the UK university admissions service; here it supplies only its inner letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Capacity is the amount of room a place has, the space there is to fill.

clue.text: Top club, perhaps on island

parts.note: a club is one suit of playing card; 'perhaps' flags an example
I is the standard abbreviation for island

explanation.surface: Praise for the best nightclub, maybe on some holiday island.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Top club' reads as the best nightclub, but 'Top' is a garment and 'club' a playing card.
explanation.definitionFit: A cardi, short for cardigan, is a knitted top.

clue.text: Working uptown, crew expanded

indicators.note: working the letters over remakes them into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
an eight is a rowing crew of eight oarsmen

explanation.surface: A rowing crew, now working uptown, has grown in size.
explanation.walkthrough: In rowing, an eight is a boat crewed by eight oarsmen.
explanation.definitionFit: To put on weight is to get fatter, so a body that has done so has grown bigger.

clue.text: Destructive caterpillar couple fed to dog back on farm

indicators.note: the couple goes inside the dog, like food

parts.note: a cur is a mongrel dog, opened up
a couple is two

indicators.note: take the back, the last letter, of FARM

parts.note: the last letter of FARM

explanation.surface: A farm dog being fed a pair of pests.
explanation.walkthrough: The farm scene fits the pest; the cutworm is a moth caterpillar that chews seedlings through at the base.
explanation.definitionFit: Cutworms are caterpillars that cut young plants off at ground level.

clue.text: Figure of speech in telegraphist's last cable

indicators.note: take the final letter of TELEGRAPHIST

parts.note: the last letter of TELEGRAPHIST
a cable is a thick rope

explanation.surface: A turn of phrase in the final telegram a telegraph operator sent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cable' sits in a telegraph clue so it reads as a telegram; it is the thick rope.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym from rhetoric, where the word covers any figurative turn such as metaphor or irony.

clue.text: Part-time judge dealing with injunction catches cold

parts.note: re means concerning, dealing with
an injunction is a court order
C for cold, as on taps

explanation.surface: A judge handling a court injunction while nursing a cold.
explanation.walkthrough: In England and Wales a recorder is a barrister or solicitor who sits as a judge part-time, so the legal surface is also the answer's world.
explanation.definitionFit: A British legal title: in England and Wales, practising lawyers sit as judges for a few weeks a year under this name.

clue.text: Art one suffers for — bric-a-brac likewise?

parts.note: tat is cheap junk, bric-a-brac
too means also, likewise

explanation.surface: A wry aside that suffering for your art applies to cheap ornaments as well.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Suffering for one's art' is usually a figure of speech; with a tattoo the suffering is the needle.
explanation.definitionFit: A tattoo is body art that hurts to acquire.

clue.text: German agreed, maniac in novel is wrecking story

parts.note: ja is German for yes

indicators.note: novel as an adjective means new, so the letters of MANIAC IN take a new form

parts.note: anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A German agrees that a madman in a novel is ruining the story.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Novel' seems to name the book; it is an anagram indicator. The story is Daphne du Maurier's Cornish tale of wreckers who lure ships onto rocks.
explanation.definitionFit: Jamaica Inn is du Maurier's novel about a gang of ship-wreckers.

clue.text: Burn carbon on standard tariff

parts.note: C is the chemical symbol for carbon
used as itself
a standard is a flag
a tariff is a rate charged

explanation.surface: Burning carbon billed at the ordinary energy tariff.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Standard tariff' reads as a single utility phrase; it splits into two separate pieces, FLAG and RATE.
explanation.definitionFit: A rare but plain synonym, the verb behind conflagration, a great fire.

clue.text: Poem for recital not settled yet

indicators.note: a recital is spoken out loud, so take the sound

parts.note: an ode is a poem

explanation.surface: A poem meant for performance whose words are still not final.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Settled' reads as a draft being finalised; it is a bill being paid.
explanation.definitionFit: Money still due on an unpaid bill: a debt not yet settled is outstanding.

clue.text: Tied in knots, prepare for release

indicators.note: letters tied in knots are tangled out of order

parts.note: anagram fodder

explanation.surface: Someone bound up in knots getting ready to be freed.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface makes 'release' freedom from bonds; it is the release of a book or film.
explanation.definitionFit: Editing a text or film prepares it for publication.

clue.text: Bottom section of genuine Thermos twists

indicators.note: the answer is a section of the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run from the end of 'genuine', through 'Thermos', to the first letter of 'twists'

explanation.surface: The base of a real vacuum flask screws on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Twists' looks like an anagram indicator for Thermos; it only supplies the final T.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain, rather archaic synonym for lowest, built on 'nether' as in the nether regions.

clue.text: Bonus point

definitions.meaning: extra money given for good service

explanation.walkthrough: The slash in the printed clue marks the split between the two definitions.
explanation.definitionFit: A tip is a gratuity, a bonus; it is also a point, as in the tip of a pen.

clue.text: Penny cracking cryptic clues had to guess

indicators.note: the penny cracks open the other letters and sits inside them
cryptic means obscure or puzzling, so the letters are scrambled

parts.note: taken as written
had a meal means ate

explanation.surface: Penny, working through some cryptic clues, was forced to guess.
explanation.walkthrough: Penny looks like a solver's name, but it is the coin abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: To speculate is to form a theory without firm evidence, a conjecture.

clue.text: Might forager bring home the bacon, after taking this out?

definitions.text: Might forager bring home the bacon
definitions.meaning: the surface reading: would a foraging animal earn its keep? 'Bring home the bacon' is an idiom for earning a living
the setter's reading: remove the first word of the answer's name and what is left is literally a pig, the source of bacon

explanation.surface: A question about whether a foraging animal would still earn its keep once something is removed.
explanation.walkthrough: A truffle pig is a forager that finds truffles; take TRUFFLE out of its name and PIG is left, which is literally bacon. 'Bring home the bacon' means earn a living.
explanation.definitionFit: Truffle pigs are used to sniff out and dig up truffles.

clue.text: Loud blowing to cool food down?

parts.note: to fan something is to cool it
fare is food

explanation.surface: Blowing hard on a hot dish to cool it before eating.
explanation.walkthrough: The blowing looks like breath over hot food; it is trumpets. 'Down' just places FAN above FARE in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: A fanfare is a loud flourish blown on trumpets.

clue.text: How much fun this is? Very little, you'd say

indicators.note: said out loud, one word sounds like another

parts.note: wee is Scottish and British for very small

explanation.surface: A dry reply to a question about how enjoyable something is: hardly at all.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the exclamation itself: 'whee!' is what you say when having fun, so 'this' is the word.
explanation.definitionFit: Whee is a cry of delight, how you express fun.

clue.text: Test team declines after success

parts.note: a win is a success
to die away is to decline

explanation.surface: A sports side that fades after winning.
explanation.walkthrough: The Windies is the nickname of the West Indies cricket team, which plays Test (five-day international) matches; 'declines' also sounds like a cricket declaration.
explanation.definitionFit: The Windies are the West Indies, a Test-playing cricket nation.

clue.text: Man advancing by single steps north on foot

parts.note: a paw is an animal's foot
N is the abbreviation for north; placed after PAW

explanation.surface: A man walking north step by step.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Man' is a chess piece, and a pawn moves one square at a time; 'north on foot' puts N after PAW in an across answer.
explanation.definitionFit: In chess the pawn is a man that advances one square at a time.

clue.text: Mud bricks are good enough in Lincoln?

indicators.note: 'in' places the phrase for 'good enough' inside the name that Lincoln stands for

parts.note: ABE, Abraham Lincoln's nickname, opened up
'that will do' means it is good enough

explanation.surface: Asking whether mud bricks would pass muster in the English city of Lincoln.
explanation.walkthrough: Lincoln looks like the English cathedral city; it is Abraham Lincoln, US president, known as Abe.
explanation.definitionFit: Adobe is sun-dried mud brick.

clue.text: Ice creams in Rome? We in Paris like jelly

parts.note: gelati is Italian for ice creams
nous is French for we

explanation.surface: A tourist compares Roman ice cream to a Parisian's liking for jelly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Like' reads as the verb, the French liking jelly; it belongs to the definition and means resembling.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the word comes from gelatine, the setting agent in jelly.

clue.text: Regretful having traded small for large vehicle

indicators.note: one letter is traded for another, so it is swapped out
for names what the traded letter is exchanged with, its replacement

parts.note: sorry means regretful
S is the clothing abbreviation for small
L is the clothing abbreviation for large

explanation.surface: Someone sorry for swapping a small car for a big one.
explanation.walkthrough: Small and large are clothing sizes here; lorry is the British word for a truck.
explanation.definitionFit: A lorry is the British word for a truck, a large goods vehicle.

clue.text: Moonlight, say, really a result of sunlight reflected

parts.note: 'so good' means really good

indicators.note: a reflection shows things back to front

parts.note: used as itself
a suntan

explanation.surface: Moonlight explained as really being sunlight bounced back off the moon.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface's science is true, which disguises 'Moonlight' as Beethoven's Moonlight Sonata; 'say' flags it as an example.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Beethoven's Piano Sonata No 14 is nicknamed the Moonlight.

clue.text: Playwright having Jack return with different giant

indicators.note: to return is to go back, so the letters are read backwards

parts.note: a jack tar, or tar, is a sailor

indicators.note: a different form of the word means its letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A dramatist whose play brings Jack back, alongside a different giant.
explanation.walkthrough: Jack and the giant suggest the beanstalk tale, but Jack here is a sailor.
explanation.definitionFit: Terence Rattigan was an English dramatist, author of The Winslow Boy and The Browning Version.

clue.text: Pet that won't get pregnant until married

parts.note: from nine to five = from nine until five
m is the abbreviation for married

explanation.surface: A prim rule that a pet should not become pregnant before marriage.
explanation.walkthrough: The moral tone is the joke; a tom is a male cat, which can never get pregnant.
explanation.definitionFit: A tom is a male cat, a pet that cannot be pregnant.

clue.text: Measure yard next to church; ie the churchyard

definitions.note: 'the churchyard' names one burial ground, as the answer is used with an article

indicators.note: the church abbreviation sits right beside the measure and yard, ahead of them

parts.note: CE is the Church of England
a meter measures, as a gas meter does
y is the abbreviation for yard

explanation.surface: A surveyor measuring the yard beside a church, which is to say the churchyard.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue seems to define itself twice over; 'yard' is really just the letter Y, and 'measure' uses the US spelling of the device that measures.
explanation.definitionFit: A near synonym: a churchyard is the burial ground around a church, and the answer is any burial ground.

clue.text: Miles one travels across snow, given wrong directions

parts.note: m is the abbreviation for miles
I is the Roman numeral one
to sled is to travel by sledge

explanation.surface: A long snowy trek made after being pointed the wrong way.
explanation.walkthrough: SLED is the verb here, past tense of travelling on a sledge, which is how 'travels' fits.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the past participle: led astray, pointed the wrong way.
